Request Appointment Chronic bladder infection: Is there a cure? Products and services Why are women more likely to have chronic bladder infections? What can be done about them? A bladder infection is a type of urinary tract infection (UTI). You might have chronic, or recurrent, bladder infections if you have two or more bladder infections in six months or three or more infections in a year. Several factors make women more likely to have recurrent bladder infections. These factors include: * Having kidney or bladder stones. * Bacteria getting into the urethra during sex. The urethra is the passage that allows urine to exit the body. * Changing estrogen levels during menopause. * Problems with the urinary tract shape or function. * An inherited risk of developing bladder infections. Tests to find the cause of recurrent bladder infections may include: * Collecting a urine sample for a urine culture test to see what bacteria may be causing infection * A visual exam of the bladder and urethra with a lighted device (cystoscopy) * A computerized tomography (CT) scan of the urinary tract Treatment is directed at the underlying cause, when possible. If an underlying cause can't be found, one of these treatments may help: * A low-dose antibiotic taken for at least six months and up to two years * Intermittent or self-directed antibiotic therapy — for instance, taking an antibiotic after sex or starting a course of antibiotics at the first sign of a UTI * Vaginal estrogen therapy for signs or symptoms related to vaginal dryness after menopause Expert opinions vary on whether certain lifestyle changes reduce the risk of bladder infection. It may be helpful to: * Drink plenty of liquids, especially water, to help flush out bacteria * Urinate often, especially when you feel the need * Wipe from front to back after urinating or having a bowel movement * Take showers rather than baths * Gently wash the skin around your vagina and anus daily using a mild soap and plenty of water * Use forms of birth control other than a diaphragm and spermicides * Empty your bladder as soon as possible after sex * Avoid using deodorant sprays or scented feminine products in the genital area Some studies have shown that cranberry products may have infection-fighting properties to help prevent urinary tract infections. Kim; Erin Kirkby, MS SUMMARY Purpose Over the past few decades, our ability to diagnose, treat, and manage recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) long-term has evolved due to additional insights into the pathophysiology of rUTI, a new appreciation for the adverse effects of repetitive antimicrobial therapy (“collateral damage”),1 rising rates of bacterial antimicrobial resistance, and better reporting of the natural history and clinical outcomes of acute cystitis and rUTI. For the purposes of this Guideline, the Panel considers only recurrent episodes of localized (restricted to the lower urinary tract) cystitis in women. This Guideline does not apply to individuals with complicating factors that place them at higher risk for development of a urinary tract infection (UTI) or for decreased efficacy of therapy as well as those with signs or symptoms of systemic bacteremia. In this document, the term UTI will refer to acute bacterial cystitis unless otherwise specified. This document seeks to establish guidance for the evaluation and management of patients with rUTIs to prevent inappropriate use of antibiotics, decrease the risk of antibiotic resistance, reduce adverse effects of antibiotic use, provide guidance on antibiotic and non-antibiotic strategies for prevention, and improve clinical outcomes and quality of life for women with rUTIs by reducing recurrence of UTI events. Methodology The systematic review utilized to inform this Guideline was conducted by a methodology team at the Pacific Northwest Evidence-based Practice Center (EPC). Scoping of the report and review of the final systematic review to inform Guideline statements was conducted in conjunction with the rUTI Panel. A research librarian conducted searches in Ovid MEDLINE (1946 to January [Week 1] 2018), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (through December 2017) and Embase (through January 16, 2018). Searches of electronic databases were supplemented by reviewing reference lists of relevant articles. An update literature search was conducted on September 20, 2018. In 2022, the EPC conducted an update review assessing abstracts from new studies published since the publication of the 2019 Guideline. The American Urological Association (AUA) asked the EPC to further assess a subset of studies included in the update report, to support potential changes to the 2019 Guideline. In 2025, the rUTI Guideline was updated through the AUA amendment process in which newly published literature were reviewed and integrated into previously published Guidelines. The methodologist searched for studies published on or after June 1, 2021 to November 1, 2024 using the same PubMed search strategies and strings from 2019 that were used for the original rUTI evidence report. New searches were constructed for new Key Questions addressing next generation sequencing and other non-culture testing, as well as for an existing Key Question to capture symptoms predictive of a UTI requiring treatment. Clinicians should obtain urinalysis, urine culture and sensitivity with each symptomatic acute cystitis episode prior to initiating treatment in patients with rUTIs. (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C) 3. To make a diagnosis of rUTI, clinicians should document evidence of inflammation (pyuria) and the presence of uropathogenic bacteria in association with symptomatic episodes. (Clinical Principle) 4. Clinicians should obtain repeat urine studies when an initial urine specimen is suspect for contamination, with consideration for obtaining a catheterized specimen. (Clinical Principle) 5. Cystoscopy and upper tract imaging should not be routinely obtained in the index patient presenting with rUTI. (Expert Opinion) 6. Clinicians may offer patient-initiated treatment (self-start treatment) to select rUTI patients with acute episodes while awaiting urine cultures. (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C) Asymptomatic Bacteriuria 7. Clinicians should omit surveillance urine testing, including urine culture, in asymptomatic patients with rUTIs. (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C) 8. Clinicians should not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in patients. (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B) Antibiotic Treatment 9. Clinicians should treat rUTI patients experiencing acute cystitis episodes with as short a duration of antibiotics as reasonable, generally no longer than seven days. fetched_contents.text: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) in Males Workup: Approach Considerations, Urine Studies, Imaging Studies Workup Approach Considerations The workup of urinary tract infections (UTIs) is dependent on the suspected diagnosis. Urinalysis, Gram staining, and urine culture should always be obtained. The threshold for establishing true UTI includes documenting 2-5 or more white blood cells (WBCs) or 15 bacteria per high-power field (HPF) in a centrifuged urine sediment. As with females, a positive nitrite test is poorly sensitive but highly specific for UTI. False positives are uncommon. Low-grade proteinuria commonly occurs in UTIs. ### What the tests and specialist evaluation would show

For recurrent UTIs, the most useful lab tests are **urinalysis**, **urine culture**, and **Gram staining**. Medscape notes that urinalysis, Gram staining, and urine culture should always be obtained, and urine culture is especially important because it helps identify the bacteria causing the infection and guide antibiotic choice [N3-R2]. The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline reinforces this by recommending urinalysis and urine culture and sensitivity with each symptomatic acute cystitis episode in patients with recurrent UTIs [N3-F2]. It also says clinicians should repeat urine studies when an initial specimen is suspect for contamination and may consider a catheterized specimen [N3-F2]. This is important because recurrent negative urine cultures can still be meaningful if the symptoms are persistent or if the culture was obtained under conditions that may have missed low-grade colonization or contamination [N3-F2].

For diagnosis and recurrence risk, the guideline emphasizes that a diagnosis of rUTI should be based on evidence of inflammation (pyuria) and the presence of uropathogenic bacteria in association with symptomatic episodes [N3-F2]. It also notes that **urine culture remains the gold standard** for the diagnosis of UTI [N3-F3]. In men, urine cultures are typically interpreted using colony-forming units per milliliter, with thresholds for positivity, although the exact number is somewhat controversial and may vary depending on the setting and whether symptoms are present [N3-F3]. In women, the same principle applies, but the guideline explicitly focuses on localized lower urinary tract cystitis rather than upper tract infections [N3-F2].

Imaging or specialist referral is generally **not routine** in the index patient with recurrent UTI, according to the AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline, which says cystoscopy and upper tract imaging should not be routinely obtained in the index patient presenting with rUTI [N3-F2]. That said, imaging may still be needed in patients with **red flags** such as recurrent infection, persistent symptoms, or risk factors for upper tract disease. The Medscape workup source notes that imaging should be considered in patients with a history of kidney stones, especially struvite stones, diabetes, polycystic kidneys, tuberculosis, or other conditions that raise the risk of obstructive disease, abscess formation, or structural complications [N3-F3]. It also suggests that imaging may be needed in patients with suspected obstructive uropathy, especially in the emergency setting, because obstructive nephrolithiasis is an emergent condition [N3-F3].

Recurrent negative urine cultures and persistent symptoms are a key diagnostic challenge. The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline says clinicians should repeat urine studies when an initial specimen is suspect for contamination [N3-F2]. It also says clinicians may offer patient-initiated treatment while awaiting urine cultures [N3-F2]. This is important because persistent symptoms can sometimes point to **recurrent or chronic colonization**, **persistent low-grade infection**, **anatomical obstruction**, or **noninfectious pelvic pain** [N2-R3][N7-R2][N7-R3]. In other words, negative cultures do not always rule out a problem; they may simply mean the infection was not captured on that particular specimen or that the cause is not bacterial [N3-F2].

So, the specialist evaluation would likely include:
- a complete patient history and pelvic examination [N3-F2],
- urinalysis and urine culture [N3-R2][N3-F2],
- repeat testing if the initial specimen is suspect for contamination [N3-F2],
- imaging if there are red flags such as stones, diabetes, or structural disease [N3-F3],
- and consideration of specialist referral if symptoms persist after appropriate testing or if there is suspicion of chronic low-grade infection, anatomical abnormality, or nerve-related symptoms [N3-F2][N3-F3].

In short, the tests are useful for confirming infection, guiding treatment, and identifying recurrence risk, while imaging and specialist referral are reserved for patients with red flags or persistent symptoms after standard evaluation [N3-R2][N3-F2][N3-F3].

### Treatment and prevention options the patient can understand

For recurrent bladder infections, the main treatment strategy is to treat the **current episode** and then decide whether to use **prophylaxis**. The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline recommends using first-line therapy such as nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), or fosfomycin, depending on the local antibiogram [N3-F2]. It also says clinicians should treat acute cystitis episodes with as short a duration of antibiotics as reasonable, generally no longer than seven days [N3-F2]. That means short-term treatment is usually limited to a course of antibiotics for the current infection.

Long-term treatment is usually **antibiotic prophylaxis**, but the guideline is careful to emphasize that it is not the default for everyone. It states that long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis is effective but requires high patient compliance and risks resistance, and patients may relapse when prophylaxis is stopped [N5-R1]. In practice, the guideline supports both **continuous prophylaxis** and **postcoital prophylaxis**, with the latter appearing to have similar effectiveness [N5-R5]. It also notes that all patients on prophylaxis should be reviewed every 3 months by the prescriber, with clinical reassessment [N5-R4]. That means long-term treatment is usually used only after careful evaluation and is not indefinite; it is meant to reduce recurrence, not to be used forever without review.

Prevention methods that are practical and evidence-based include:
- **drinking plenty of fluids, especially water**, which helps flush bacteria from the urinary tract [N1-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5],
- **urinating after intercourse**, which is a common behavioral recommendation [N6-R4],
- **not delaying urination**, **wiping front to back**, and **avoiding tight clothing** [N6-R4],
- **emptying the bladder as soon as possible after sex** [N2-F1],
- **avoiding deodorant sprays or scented feminine products in the genital area** [N2-F1],
- **gently washing the skin around the vagina and anus daily with mild soap and plenty of water** [N2-F1].

The evidence is strongest for hydration, frequent urination, and hygiene practices rather than for any single non-antibiotic remedy. The Mayo Clinic source also notes that evidence for cranberry products is limited and inconsistent, so it should not be treated as a reliable prevention strategy [N2-F1]. That makes the practical prevention advice simple and focused on reducing exposure and flushing the tract.

When to stop or adjust treatment depends on whether the symptoms are resolved and whether the patient is still at risk. The guideline says clinicians should repeat urine studies when an initial specimen is suspect for contamination and may consider catheterized specimens [N3-F2]. It also says clinicians may offer patient-initiated treatment while awaiting urine cultures [N3-F2]. In other words, if symptoms improve after a short course of antibiotics, that is a good sign that the infection was the main issue. If symptoms recur despite treatment, prophylaxis may be considered [N5-R1]. If symptoms persist after appropriate testing and treatment, the patient should see a specialist [N4-R2][N4-R5].

When to seek specialist care is important. The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline does not explicitly say to see a urologist for every recurrence, but it does emphasize specialist evaluation when cystoscopy or imaging is needed [N3-F2]. The urology-related sources also say that UTIs can become serious when the infection spreads to the blood and causes sepsis, which is a reason to seek care immediately [N4-R2]. In addition, the guideline says that clinicians should obtain a complete patient history and perform a pelvic examination in women with rUTIs [N3-F2], which is a sign that specialist-level evaluation may be needed when symptoms are persistent or recurrent [N4-R5].

So the patient can understand this as:
- **short-term treatment**: take a short course of antibiotics for the current infection [N3-F2],
- **long-term treatment**: low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis only if needed and reviewed regularly [N5-R1][N5-R4],
- **prevention**: drink plenty of water, urinate after sex, wipe front to back, and avoid irritating products [N1-R1][N6-R4][N2-F1],
- **when to adjust**: review prophylaxis every 3 months and reassess if symptoms recur or persist [N5-R4],
- **when to see a specialist**: if symptoms don’t improve after treatment, if there are red flags, or if recurrent infections are not responding well [N3-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Likely medical causes of recurrent infections and pain

The most likely medical causes fall into four broad categories: **urological causes**, **gynecological causes**, **chronic low-grade infection or persistent colonization**, and **noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms**.

#### 1) Urological causes
Urological causes include **bladder stones**, **anatomical abnormalities**, and **catheter use**. The Mayo Clinic source says that recurrent bladder infections may be caused by kidney or bladder stones, and the Cleveland Clinic source defines recurrent UTIs as two or more infections within six months or three or more within a year [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline also notes that the definition of rUTI applies to localized lower urinary tract cystitis in women and does not cover complicating factors that increase infection risk or reduce therapy efficacy [N3-F2]. That means anatomical issues such as stones, structural abnormalities, or catheter use can be important contributors to recurrent infection [N2-R1][N3-F2]. Imaging may be needed in patients with red flags such as stones, diabetes, polycystic kidneys, or tuberculosis, but it is not routine in the index patient [N3-F3].

#### 2) Gynecological causes
Gynecological causes include **vaginal infections**, **menopause**, and **pelvic organ prolapse**. The Mayo Clinic source lists changing estrogen levels during menopause as a factor that increases the risk of recurrent bladder infections [N2-F1]. It also recommends vaginal estrogen therapy for signs or symptoms related to vaginal dryness after menopause [N2-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source similarly notes that recurrent UTIs are not due to poor hygiene or behavior and that some women are simply prone to them [N2-R2]. That suggests hormonal and gynecological changes can make the urinary tract more vulnerable to recurrent infection [N2-R2][N2-F1]. Pelvic organ prolapse may also affect bladder function and increase the risk of infection or symptoms, though the evidence in the provided material is indirect [N2-R1][N2-F1].

#### 3) Chronic low-grade infection or persistent colonization
Chronic low-grade infection or persistent colonization can be a possible explanation for recurrent infections, especially when symptoms persist after treatment. The evidence from the chronic bladder infection source says that tests may include urine culture, cystoscopy, and CT scan if an underlying cause is suspected [N2-F1]. The recurrent UTI literature also suggests that chronic low-grade bacterial bladder colonization may exacerbate overactive bladder symptoms and could be the etiology of recurrent UTI [N2-R3]. In other words, some patients may have ongoing bacterial presence in the bladder that is not easily detected by a single culture or that persists even after antibiotic treatment [N2-R3].

#### 4) Noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms
Noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms can mimic UTIs. The Duke Health news article says that recurrent UTIs can lead to lingering symptoms such as chronic pelvic pain and urinary frequency even after antibiotics [N7-R1]. Another source suggests that recurrent infections drive persistent bladder dysfunction and pain via **sensory nerve sprouting and mast cell activity** [N7-R2]. A Scientific American article similarly says that UTI symptoms can resurface long after bacteria are gone, and a new study suggests nerve growth is to blame [N7-R3]. Pelvic nerve pain is also discussed in a urology resource, which notes referred pain and pelvic nerve pain as relevant to chronic UTI care [N7-R4]. These findings suggest that some patients may continue to have pain or urinary symptoms even if the infection itself is no longer present [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

In summary, recurrent infections and pain may be caused by:
- **bladder stones, anatomical abnormalities, or catheter use**,
- **vaginal infections, menopause, or pelvic organ prolapse**,
- **chronic low-grade infection or persistent colonization**, and
- **noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F1][N2-R3][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

### Patient-facing explanation of next steps and specialist care

#### What to do now to reduce risk and improve symptoms
The most practical steps to reduce risk and improve symptoms are simple but important:
- **Drink plenty of fluids, especially water**, to help flush bacteria from the urinary tract [N1-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Urinate after intercourse**, which is a common and evidence-backed practice [N6-R4].
- **Empty the bladder as soon as possible after sex** [N2-F1].
- **Wipe front to back** after urinating or having a bowel movement [N6-R4].
- **Avoid tight clothing, deodorant sprays, and scented feminine products** in the genital area [N2-F1].
- **Gently wash the skin around the vagina and anus daily with mild soap and plenty of water** [N2-F1].
- **Not delay urination** [N6-R4].

These steps are practical and evidence-based, and they can help prevent new infections and reduce the likelihood of recurrent pain [N1-R1][N6-R4][N2-F1]. If symptoms are already present, the patient should also treat the current infection promptly, using the right antibiotics as prescribed.

#### When to see a primary care provider versus a urologist
A primary care provider is usually the first place to go when the patient has **current symptoms of a UTI**, such as **painful urination**, **frequent urination**, **a burning sensation when peeing**, or **lower abdominal pain** [N4-R1]. The provider can:
- do a **urinalysis and urine culture** [N3-R2][N3-F2],
- prescribe short-term antibiotic treatment [N3-F2],
- and decide whether prophylaxis is needed [N5-R1][N5-R5].

A urologist should be seen if:
- the infections are **recurrent** or **not responding well to treatment** [N4-R2][N4-R5],
- there are **red flags** such as fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, back pain, blood in the urine, or pregnancy [N4-R5],
- the patient has **persistent symptoms** even after appropriate testing [N3-F2],
- or the provider suspects an **anatomical issue**, **chronic low-grade infection**, or **nerve-related pain** [N2-R3][N7-R2][N7-R3].

In short, start with the primary care provider for the current episode and recurrent symptoms; see a urologist if symptoms persist, recur despite treatment, or if there are signs that something more serious is going on [N4-R2][N4-R5].

#### What specialist evaluation might include and why it matters
Specialist evaluation matters because it helps find the **reason behind recurrent infections** and **persistent pain**. Based on the evidence, a urologist or specialist may:
- do a **complete patient history and pelvic examination** [N3-F2],
- repeat **urinalysis and urine culture** and consider a **catheterized specimen** if the initial culture is suspect [N3-F2],
- do **imaging** if there are red flags such as stones, diabetes, polycystic kidneys, tuberculosis, or other structural disease [N3-F3],
- consider **cystoscopy or upper tract imaging** if needed, though the guideline says these are not routine in the index patient with recurrent UTI [N3-F2][N3-F3].

Why this matters is that recurrent negative urine cultures and persistent symptoms may not mean the infection is gone; they may mean there is **chronic low-grade colonization**, **persistent infection**, **anatomical obstruction**, or **noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms** [N2-R3][N7-R2][N7-R3]. Specialist evaluation can help distinguish these possibilities and guide the right treatment [N3-F2][N3-F3].

So, the next steps are: **do the practical prevention and treatment steps now**, **see a primary care provider first** for the current episode, and **see a urologist if symptoms keep coming back, if there are red flags, or if specialist-level testing is needed** [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N3-F2][N3-F3].

Gynecological factors may also play a role. The Mayo Clinic source lists **changing estrogen levels during menopause** as a factor that increases the risk of recurrent bladder infections and recommends **vaginal estrogen therapy** for signs or symptoms related to vaginal dryness after menopause [N2-F1]. It also says that recurrent UTIs are not due to poor hygiene or behavior and that some women are simply prone to them [N2-R2]. This suggests that hormonal changes and related pelvic changes may make the urinary tract more vulnerable to infection [N2-R2][N2-F1]. Pelvic organ prolapse may also affect bladder function and increase the risk of infection or symptoms, though the evidence in the provided material is indirect [N2-R1][N2-F1].

### c) Chronic low-grade infection or persistent colonization
Another possibility is that the infection is not being fully cleared and may persist in a low-grade or persistent form. The evidence suggests that chronic low-grade bacterial bladder colonization may exacerbate overactive bladder symptoms and could be the etiology of recurrent UTI [N2-R3]. In other words, some people may have ongoing bacterial presence in the bladder that is not easily detected by a single culture or that persists even after antibiotic treatment [N2-R3].

### d) Noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms
Finally, the evidence also points to **noninfectious pelvic pain** or **nerve-related symptoms** that can mimic UTIs. A Duke Health source says that recurrent UTIs can lead to lingering symptoms such as **chronic pelvic pain** and **urinary frequency** even after antibiotics [N7-R1]. Another source suggests that recurrent infections drive persistent bladder dysfunction and pain via **sensory nerve sprouting and mast cell activity** [N7-R2]. A Scientific American article similarly says that UTI symptoms can resurface long after bacteria are gone, and a new study suggests **nerve growth** is to blame [N7-R3]. Pelvic nerve pain is also discussed in a urology resource, which notes referred pain and pelvic nerve pain as relevant to chronic UTI care [N7-R4]. This means that some patients may continue to have pain or urinary symptoms even if the infection itself is no longer present [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

## 2) What the tests and specialist evaluation would show
The most useful tests for recurrent UTIs are **urinalysis**, **urine culture**, and **Gram staining** [N3-R2][N3-F2]. Medscape says these should always be obtained, and urine culture is especially important because it helps identify the bacteria causing the infection and guide antibiotic choice [N3-R2]. The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline reinforces this by recommending urinalysis and urine culture and sensitivity with each symptomatic acute cystitis episode in patients with recurrent UTIs [N3-F2]. It also says clinicians should repeat urine studies when an initial specimen is suspect for contamination and may consider a catheterized specimen [N3-F2].

The guideline also says that **urine culture remains the gold standard** for the diagnosis of UTI [N3-F3]. In men, urine cultures are typically interpreted using colony-forming units per milliliter, with thresholds for positivity, although the exact number is somewhat controversial and may vary depending on the setting and whether symptoms are present [N3-F3]. In women, the same principle applies, but the guideline explicitly focuses on localized lower urinary tract cystitis rather than upper tract infections [N3-F2].

Imaging or specialist referral is generally **not routine** in the index patient with recurrent UTI, according to the AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline, which says **cystoscopy and upper tract imaging should not be routinely obtained** in the index patient presenting with rUTI [N3-F2]. That said, imaging may still be needed in patients with **red flags** such as recurrent infection, persistent symptoms, or risk factors for upper tract disease. The Medscape workup source notes that imaging should be considered in patients with a history of kidney stones, especially struvite stones, diabetes, polycystic kidneys, tuberculosis, or other conditions that raise the risk of obstructive disease, abscess formation, or structural complications [N3-F3]. It also suggests that imaging may be needed in patients with suspected obstructive uropathy, especially in the emergency setting, because obstructive nephrolithiasis is an emergent condition [N3-F3].

Recurrent negative urine cultures and persistent symptoms are a key diagnostic challenge. The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline says clinicians should repeat urine studies when an initial specimen is suspect for contamination [N3-F2]. It also says clinicians may offer patient-initiated treatment while awaiting urine cultures [N3-F2]. This is important because persistent symptoms can sometimes point to **recurrent or chronic colonization**, **persistent low-grade infection**, **anatomical obstruction**, or **noninfectious pelvic pain** [N2-R3][N7-R2][N7-R3]. In other words, negative cultures do not always rule out a problem; they may simply mean the infection was not captured on that particular specimen or that the cause is not bacterial [N3-F2].

## 3) Treatment and prevention options
The evidence supports a clear treatment approach: **treat the current episode**, then decide whether to use **prophylaxis** if needed [N3-F2][N5-R1][N5-R5].

### a) Short-term treatment
For the current infection, the AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline recommends using first-line therapy such as nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), or fosfomycin, depending on the local antibiogram [N3-F2]. It also says clinicians should treat acute cystitis episodes with as short a duration of antibiotics as reasonable, generally no longer than seven days [N3-F2]. That means short-term treatment is usually limited to a course of antibiotics for the current infection.

### b) Long-term treatment
Long-term treatment is usually **antibiotic prophylaxis**, but the evidence is cautious. It says long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis is effective but requires high patient compliance and risks resistance, and patients may relapse when prophylaxis is stopped [N5-R1]. In practice, the evidence supports both **continuous prophylaxis** and **postcoital prophylaxis**, with the latter appearing to have similar effectiveness [N5-R5]. It also notes that all patients on prophylaxis should be reviewed every 3 months by the prescriber, with clinical reassessment [N5-R4]. That means long-term treatment is usually used only after careful evaluation and is not indefinite; it is meant to reduce recurrence, not to be used forever without review [N5-R1][N5-R4].

### c) Practical prevention methods
The most practical prevention methods are simple and evidence-based:
- **Drink plenty of fluids, especially water**, to help flush bacteria from the urinary tract [N1-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5],
- **urinate after intercourse**, which is a common and evidence-backed practice [N6-R4],
- **empty the bladder as soon as possible after sex** [N2-F1],
- **wipe front to back** after urinating or having a bowel movement [N6-R4],
- **avoid tight clothing, deodorant sprays, and scented feminine products** in the genital area [N2-F1],
- **gently wash the skin around the vagina and anus daily with mild soap and plenty of water** [N2-F1],
- **not delay urination** [N6-R4].

These steps are practical and evidence-based, and they can help prevent new infections and reduce the likelihood of recurrent pain [N1-R1][N6-R4][N2-F1]. The evidence is strongest for hydration, frequent urination, and hygiene practices rather than for any single non-antibiotic remedy. The Mayo Clinic source also notes that evidence for cranberry products is limited and inconsistent, so it should not be treated as a reliable prevention strategy [N2-F1].

### d) When to stop or adjust treatment
If symptoms improve after a short course of antibiotics, that is a good sign that the infection was the main issue. If symptoms recur despite treatment, prophylaxis may be considered [N5-R1]. If symptoms persist after appropriate testing and treatment, the patient should see a specialist [N4-R2][N4-R5]. The guideline also says clinicians should repeat urine studies when an initial specimen is suspect for contamination and may consider catheterized specimens [N3-F2].

## 4) Next steps and when to see a specialist
### a) What to do now
Right now, the best approach is to:
- treat the current infection promptly with the right antibiotics,
- do the practical prevention steps such as staying hydrated, urinating after sex, wiping front to back, and avoiding irritating products [N1-R1][N6-R4][N2-F1],
- and watch for symptoms that require urgent care.

### b) When to see a primary care provider
A primary care provider is usually the first place to go when the patient has **current symptoms of a UTI**, such as **painful urination**, **frequent urination**, **a burning sensation when peeing**, or **lower abdominal pain** [N4-R1]. The provider can:
- do a **urinalysis and urine culture** [N3-R2][N3-F2],
- prescribe short-term antibiotic treatment [N3-F2],
- and decide whether prophylaxis is needed [N5-R1][N5-R5].

### c) When to see a urologist
A urologist should be seen if:
- the infections are **recurrent** or **not responding well to treatment** [N4-R2][N4-R5],
- there are **red flags** such as fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, back pain, blood in the urine, or pregnancy [N4-R5],
- the patient has **persistent symptoms** even after appropriate testing [N3-F2],
- or the provider suspects an **anatomical issue**, **chronic low-grade infection**, or **nerve-related pain** [N2-R3][N7-R2][N7-R3].

### d) What specialist evaluation might include and why it matters
Specialist evaluation matters because it helps find the **reason behind recurrent infections** and **persistent pain**. A urologist or specialist may:
- do a **complete patient history and pelvic examination** [N3-F2],
- repeat **urinalysis and urine culture** and consider a **catheterized specimen** if the initial culture is suspect [N3-F2],
- do **imaging** if there are red flags such as stones, diabetes, polycystic kidneys, tuberculosis, or other structural disease [N3-F3],
- consider **cystoscopy or upper tract imaging** if needed, though the guideline says these are not routine in the index patient with recurrent UTI [N3-F2][N3-F3].

Why this matters is that recurrent negative urine cultures and persistent symptoms may not mean the infection is gone; they may mean there is **chronic low-grade colonization**, **persistent infection**, **anatomical obstruction**, or **noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms** [N2-R3][N7-R2][N7-R3]. Specialist evaluation can help distinguish these possibilities and guide the right treatment [N3-F2][N3-F3].

## 5) Bottom line
Your mom’s bladder infections and pain when she pees may be caused by:
- **bladder stones, anatomical abnormalities, or catheter use**,
- **vaginal infections, menopause, or pelvic organ prolapse**,
- **chronic low-grade infection or persistent colonization**, or
- **noninfectious pelvic pain or nerve-related symptoms** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N3-F2][N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

The best next steps are:
- treat the current infection promptly,
- use practical prevention steps such as staying hydrated and urinating after sex,
- and see a primary care provider first,
- and then see a urologist if symptoms recur, persist, or if there are red flags [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

In short, recurrent UTIs can have many causes, and specialist evaluation is important because it can help find the right cause and the right treatment [N3-F2][N3-F3].
